title: Asking Good Questions of Your Data

production_notes: [VERSION] File upload and analysis features in Claude and ChatGPT, including free plan limits, must be checked against the live tools before recording.

Sofia, the Mexico City courier company and the deliveries file are fictional and anonymised. content.md gives no zone results, so the video shows a placeholder table with zone names only and no late percentages; do not invent figures on screen.
Scene 11 and 12 slides show Sofia's second prompt word for word as in content.md. Scene 14 slide shows the check formula =COUNTA(A2:A5000) on screen, not read aloud.
Stock footage of couriers must show no company names or logos.

Hook.voiceover: Two people upload the same file to one AI tool. One gets a vague paragraph that could fit any business. The other gets a clear table with exact numbers and a note on how they were calculated. The difference is not the tool. It is the prompt.

Explain.voiceover: Last week, you prepared clean, safe data. This week, we analyse it, and that starts with the prompt.

slide.title: Asking Good Questions of Your Data
slide.body: AI-Powered Data Analysis (No Code) · Lesson 6 of 14 · Week 2

Explain.voiceover: In lesson three, you turned a business question into a measurable data question. Now you put that question into a prompt. A strong analysis prompt has four parts. First, describe the dataset. For example, this file has ten orders from January to March twenty twenty-six, one row per order. Second, name the columns. Revenue is in column G, in US dollars.

slide.title: Four parts of an analysis prompt
slide.body: Four stacked blocks, first two lit: 1. Describe the dataset: 'This file has 10 orders from January to March 2026, one row per order.' · 2. Name the columns: 'Revenue is in column G, in US dollars. Region is in column C.' · 3. State the question (dimmed) · 4. Ask for the method (dimmed)

Explain.voiceover: Third, state the question, with the measure, group, period and comparison. What was total revenue per region for January to March? Fourth, ask for the method. Show the table first. Then tell me how many rows and which columns you used, and how you calculated each number.

slide.title: Four parts of an analysis prompt
slide.body: Blocks 3 and 4 now lit: 3. State the question: 'What was total Revenue per Region for January to March 2026?' · 4. Ask for the method: 'Show the table first. Then tell me how many rows you used, which columns, and how you calculated each number.'

Explain.voiceover: Asking for a table first, and conclusions second, is important. A table is easy to check against your own data. A paragraph of conclusions is easy to believe, and hard to check.

slide.title: Table first, conclusions second
slide.body: Table: easy to check (teal tick) | Paragraph: easy to believe, hard to check (amber warning)

Explain.voiceover: Asking for the method helps you spot problems early. If the AI says it used nine rows, and your sheet has ten, you know something is wrong before you read any conclusion. And keep one question per prompt when you start. Long prompts with five questions often skip or mix up one part.

slide.title: Why ask for the method?
slide.body: AI: 'I used 9 rows' vs your sheet: 10 rows → something is wrong · One question per prompt when you start

Explain.voiceover: And remember the safety rule from lesson two. Upload only anonymised or fictional data, or data your organisation has approved for the tool.
Explain.on_screen_text: Anonymised, fictional or approved data only

Explain.voiceover: Asking AI about your data is like ordering at a busy counter. Something to eat, please, gets you whatever is easiest to serve. One vegetable soup, small, no bread, and the receipt, gets you exactly what you wanted, plus proof of what you paid for.
Explain.stock_query: customer ordering food at busy counter

Demonstrate.voiceover: Sofia is an operations analyst for a courier company in Mexico City. She uploads a fictional, anonymised file of deliveries. The columns are delivery ID, date, zone, promised minutes and actual minutes.

Her first prompt is short. Are our deliveries late? The AI answers with a general paragraph. Some deliveries appear to be delayed, especially at busy times. It suggests that she monitor performance. There are no numbers she can use.

slide.title: Prompt 1: vague
slide.body: Prompt: 'Are our deliveries late?' → AI: 'Some deliveries appear to be delayed, especially at busy times … monitor performance.' Red label: no numbers

Demonstrate.voiceover: So she writes a second prompt. This file has one row per delivery for March twenty twenty-six. A delivery is late when actual minutes minus promised minutes is more than ten. For each zone, count the deliveries and the late deliveries, and give the percentage late.

slide.title: Prompt 2: specific
slide.body: 'This file has one row per delivery for March 2026. A delivery is late when Actual minutes minus Promised minutes is more than 10. For each Zone, count the deliveries and the late deliveries, and give the percentage late.'

Demonstrate.voiceover: Show the table first. Then tell me how many rows you used, and how you calculated each column. Conclusion in two sentences maximum.

slide.title: Prompt 2: specific (continued)
slide.body: 'Show the table first. Then tell me how many rows you used and how you calculated each column. Conclusion in two sentences maximum.'

Demonstrate.voiceover: This time, the AI gives a table with one row per zone, and the three numbers she asked for. It notes that it used all the rows in the file, and it shows the formula it used for late. The conclusion names the zone with the highest percentage late.

slide.title: Answer 2: a table and a method
slide.body: Placeholder table: Zone | Deliveries | Late | % late (zone rows, values greyed, no real figures) · Note: 'Used all rows' · 'Late = Actual − Promised > 10' · Two-sentence conclusion

Demonstrate.voiceover: Sofia still checks. She counts the rows in her own sheet with a COUNTA formula, and she recalculates the percentage for one zone. Both match, so she can use the table in her weekly report.

slide.title: Sofia's two checks
slide.body: =COUNTA(A2:A5000) → row count matches the AI ✓ · One zone's % late recalculated by formula ✓

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to ask for insights or interesting patterns, and accept whatever comes back. The AI then chooses the measure, the group and the period for you, often without saying so. Ask your own measurable question, and ask for the table and the method before the conclusion.
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: Ask your own question. Table first.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, a strong analysis prompt describes the dataset, names the columns, states a measurable question, and asks for the method. Second, ask for a table first and conclusions second, because tables are easier to check than sentences. Third, check the row count and columns the AI reports against your own sheet, before you trust the conclusion.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Dataset · columns · question · method. 2. Table first, conclusions second. 3. Check row count and columns before trusting the conclusion.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. In the exercise below this video, you will upload the clean orders sheet and ask three questions, using the four-part prompt. For each answer, note whether the AI showed its method. It takes about twenty-five minutes. In the next lesson, we build summaries and pivot tables. See you there.
